# README badges

Every active repository's `README.md` carries one generated block of badges directly
under its title. The block is built from facts about the repository, so a repository
only shows a badge it can honestly show, and the daily audit reports any block that has
drifted. Do not edit the block by hand: change the fact (the workflow, the license, the
Python floor) and rebuild it.

```markdown
# project-name

<!-- badges:start - generated by traction-control scripts/readme_badges.py; change the repository's facts, not this block -->
[![CI](...)](...) [![License: MIT](...)](LICENSE) [![Python 3.10+](...)](pyproject.toml) [![Coverage](...)](...)
<!-- badges:end -->
```

## The badges

| Badge | Shown when | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **CI** | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` exists | GitHub's own workflow badge for `ci.yml` on the default branch |
| **License** | GitHub detects a license | the SPDX id (`MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, ...) as a static badge linking to the license file |
| **Python** | `pyproject.toml` has a `requires-python` with a lower bound | `>=3.10` shows `3.10+`, as a static badge linking to `pyproject.toml` |
| **Coverage** | `ci.yml` turns coverage on (`coverage: true`, see [the Codecov guide](codecov.md)) | Codecov's badge for the repository |

A repository with none of these facts gets no block. Archived repositories are skipped:
GitHub makes them read-only. A license GitHub cannot identify gives no license badge,
which is a prompt to fix the `LICENSE` file, not to draw a guess.

## Private repositories

They get the same badges. Two of them work for a reason worth knowing:

- GitHub serves its own workflow badges itself with the viewer's session, so the **CI**
  badge renders in a private repository for anyone who can read it. Other sites cannot see it.
- The **license** and **Python** badges are static: they read nothing, so they always render.
- A private repository's **coverage** badge shows "unknown" unless its URL carries Codecov's
  *graph token*. That token can only draw the badge and graph (it cannot upload), and it is
  written into that repository's README. If such a repository is ever made public, replace
  the token first (regenerate it in Codecov). `apply` fetches it with the Codecov PAT in the
  vault, so nobody types it; the audit compares the block with the token masked, so a
  rotated token does not count as drift.

## Commands

```bash
scripts/readme_badges.py render --repo NAME                 # print the block
scripts/readme_badges.py check --all                        # every repository in the registry
scripts/readme_badges.py check --repo NAME --repo OTHER     # exit 1 if any block is missing or drifted
scripts/readme_badges.py apply --repo NAME --readme PATH    # write it into a local README (--dry-run to see)
```

`check` reads the README and the facts from GitHub, so it needs `gh` signed in and, for
`--all`, the visibility registry. The daily audit (`scripts/portfolio-audit.sh`) runs
`check --all` and counts each repository that needs attention.

`apply` puts a new block directly under the first `# ` title, replaces an existing block
in place (so a block someone moved stays where they put it), removes the block when no
badge applies, and refuses a README that does not start with a title instead of guessing.
It leaves badges written by hand outside the block alone and lists them, so a duplicate
can be folded in by hand; a PyPI badge, for example, is not managed.

## Changing the standard

Edit `badges()` in `scripts/readme_badges.py` and its tests, then rebuild every README with
the same sweep that introduced the block: for each repository, `apply`, run its own
pre-commit, and open a pull request. The audit shows which repositories still differ.

## Why static license and Python badges

A dynamic badge asks shields.io to read the repository, which fails for private
repositories and adds a lookup that can go stale or be rate limited. The facts are already
known here, and the audit keeps the static text honest, so the badge is drawn from them.
